questions.stem: Which characteristic is found in all living organisms but NOT in a burning candle?
questions.explanation: A burning candle also uses oxygen, gives off heat and produces CO2, but only living things can reproduce.

questions.stem: Which organelle would you expect to find in large numbers in the cells of a muscle that contracts continuously, such as heart muscle?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration and supply the ATP needed for constant contraction.

questions.stem: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall outside the cell membrane. Animal cells have no cell wall.

questions.stem: What is the main function of ribosomes?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes join amino acids together in the order coded by messenger RNA.

questions.stem: The cell walls of green plants are made mainly of
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide. Chitin is found in fungal cell walls and arthropod exoskeletons.

questions.stem: The cell walls of most fungi are made of
questions.explanation: Fungal cell walls contain chitin, which is one reason fungi are not classified as plants.

questions.stem: Which part of the cell controls its activities and contains its genetic material?
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds the chromosomes (DNA), which direct the activities of the cell.

questions.stem: Lysosomes are organelles that contain
questions.explanation: Lysosomes break down worn-out organelles and engulfed particles.

questions.stem: The Golgi apparatus (Golgi body) mainly
options: modifies, packages and secretes substances such as enzymes
questions.explanation: It processes proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum and packs them into vesicles for secretion.

questions.stem: The large central vacuole of a plant cell, filled with cell sap, helps the cell to
options: stay turgid, which supports the plant
questions.explanation: Water taken into the vacuole by osmosis presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall, so the cell becomes firm (turgid).

questions.stem: The cell membrane is described as selectively (partially) permeable because it
options: lets some substances through but not others
questions.explanation: This allows the cell to control what enters and leaves it.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of the levels of organisation in a multicellular organism?
questions.explanation: Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs work together in systems, and systems make up the organism.

questions.stem: Paramecium is an example of life organised at the level of
options: a single cell that performs all life processes
questions.explanation: Paramecium is unicellular. Its one cell feeds, respires, excretes and reproduces.

questions.stem: Hydra is used as an example of organisation at the tissue level because its body
options: is made of a single cell
has a well-developed heart and kidneys
has organ systems such as a digestive system with an anus
is made of layers of cells, each layer doing particular jobs, but it has no true organs
questions.explanation: Hydra has ectoderm and endoderm tissues separated by mesogloea, but no organs.

questions.stem: An onion bulb is used as an example of organisation at the level of
questions.explanation: The bulb is made of several tissues working together to store food and allow perennation.

questions.stem: The removal of the waste products of metabolism from the body is called
questions.explanation: Egestion is the removal of undigested food (faeces), which never took part in the body's metabolism.

questions.stem: Irritability (sensitivity) is the ability of an organism to
options: detect and respond to changes in its surroundings
questions.explanation: Responding to stimuli such as light, touch and chemicals helps organisms survive.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is part of the cell theory?
options: Cells are found only in animals
All living things are made of cells, and new cells come only from existing cells
questions.explanation: The cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life.

questions.stem: Colourless plastids that store starch in the cells of roots and tubers are called
questions.explanation: Chromoplasts hold coloured pigments, and chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Centrioles, found in animal cells, are involved in
options: forming the spindle during cell division
questions.explanation: In animal cells the spindle fibres grow out from the centrioles during mitosis and meiosis.

questions.stem: Which structure is ABSENT from a prokaryotic cell such as a bacterium?
questions.explanation: In prokaryotes the DNA lies free in the cytoplasm and is not enclosed in a nucleus.

questions.stem: A cell is seen to have a cellulose wall, many chloroplasts and a large central vacuole. It is most likely
options: a palisade mesophyll cell of a leaf
questions.explanation: Root hair cells have no chloroplasts, and yeast and red blood cells have neither chloroplasts nor a cellulose wall.

questions.stem: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is so called because
options: ribosomes are attached to its surface
it is covered by a cell wall
questions.explanation: Rough ER carries ribosomes and transports the proteins they make.

questions.stem: The building up of complex substances from simpler ones in living cells is called
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis and protein synthesis are anabolic processes. Catabolism is the breakdown of substances.

questions.stem: The orange and red colours of ripe fruits and many flowers are due to pigments stored in
questions.explanation: Chromoplasts contain carotenoid pigments that attract animals for pollination and seed dispersal.

questions.stem: The basic structural and functional unit of all living things is the
questions.explanation: All organisms are made up of one or more cells.

questions.stem: Blue-green algae are placed in the kingdom Monera because they
options: have no true nucleus enclosed by a membrane
questions.explanation: Members of Monera, such as bacteria and cyanobacteria, are prokaryotes.

questions.stem: Euglena is said to have both plant and animal features because it
options: has a cell wall made of cellulose and a backbone
has chloroplasts for photosynthesis but can also take in food from its surroundings and swim with a flagellum
questions.explanation: Euglena photosynthesises in light, can feed heterotrophically in darkness, and moves like an animal.

questions.stem: Paramecium moves by means of
questions.explanation: Thousands of beating cilia drive Paramecium through water.

questions.stem: Amoeba moves and captures its food by means of
questions.explanation: Pseudopodia are temporary projections of the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: Rhizopus (bread mould) reproduces asexually by
questions.explanation: The black sporangia burst and release light spores that are carried by air.

questions.stem: Fungi such as mushrooms are described as saprophytes because they
options: make their own food by photosynthesis
live inside the bodies of animals
feed on dead organic matter by secreting enzymes onto it and absorbing the products
questions.explanation: Fungi lack chlorophyll, so they digest dead material outside their bodies and absorb the soluble products.

questions.stem: Spirogyra reproduces sexually by
questions.explanation: The contents of cells in neighbouring filaments fuse through a conjugation tube to form zygospores.

questions.stem: Which group of plants has no true roots, stems or leaves and is attached to the ground by rhizoids?
questions.explanation: Bryophytes are simple land plants without vascular tissue.

questions.stem: In the life cycle of a moss, the dominant (main) plant body is the
questions.explanation: The leafy moss plant is haploid and bears the sex organs. The sporophyte grows on it and depends on it.

questions.stem: In ferns, the dominant generation is the
questions.explanation: The leafy fern plant is the diploid sporophyte. Its gametophyte (the prothallus) is small and short-lived.

questions.stem: In the life cycle of a fern, the prothallus is
options: the spore case on the underside of the leaf
a small, flat gametophyte that bears the sex organs
the young leaf of the sporophyte
questions.explanation: The prothallus produces antheridia and archegonia. After fertilisation, a new sporophyte grows from it.

questions.stem: Mosses and ferns still need water for sexual reproduction because
options: their seeds germinate only in water
their pollen is carried by water
their male gametes must swim to the egg
questions.explanation: Their motile sperm need a film of water to reach the archegonium.

questions.stem: Gymnosperms differ from angiosperms because gymnosperms
options: have flowers with brightly coloured petals
have naked seeds that are not enclosed in an ovary
questions.explanation: Gymnosperm seeds lie exposed on cone scales. Angiosperm seeds develop inside an ovary, which becomes the fruit.

questions.stem: Which of these plants is a gymnosperm?
questions.explanation: Pine is a conifer that bears its seeds in cones. Maize and mango are angiosperms, and ferns have no seeds.

questions.stem: Which pair of features is typical of a monocotyledon such as maize?
options: Network leaf veins and a tap root
Two cotyledons and a tap root
Parallel leaf veins and fibrous roots
Vascular bundles in a ring and broad leaves
questions.explanation: Monocots have one cotyledon, parallel venation, fibrous roots and scattered vascular bundles.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows plant groups in order of increasing structural complexity?
questions.explanation: The order runs from a simple alga (thallophyte), to bryophyte, to pteridophyte with vascular tissue, to seed plant.

questions.stem: True vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) first appears in which group of plants?
questions.explanation: Ferns were the first plants with true roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue.

questions.stem: The main evolutionary trend from thallophytes through bryophytes and pteridophytes to seed plants is
options: a decrease in the size of the sporophyte
a return to life in water
increasing independence from water for fertilisation
questions.explanation: Seed plants use pollen tubes to deliver male gametes, so they no longer need water for fertilisation and can live on dry land.

questions.stem: The gills on the underside of the cap of a mushroom
questions.explanation: The gills give a large surface area for producing basidiospores.

questions.stem: Bacteria usually reproduce by
questions.explanation: A bacterial cell copies its DNA and divides into two daughter cells.

questions.stem: Which of these organisms is a protophyte (a plant-like protist)?
questions.explanation: Chlamydomonas has a chloroplast and photosynthesises. The other three are protozoans.

questions.stem: Waterleaf (Talinum), a common vegetable in southern Nigeria, is classified as
questions.explanation: Waterleaf has net-veined leaves and two cotyledons, which are features of dicots.

questions.stem: Which feature of seed plants was most important in allowing them to colonise dry land successfully?
options: The pollen tube, which carries male gametes to the ovule without the need for water
questions.explanation: The pollen tube, together with a protective seed, removed the need for water during fertilisation.

questions.stem: Paramecium keeps a fixed shape, unlike Amoeba, because it has
options: a firm outer covering called the pellicle
questions.explanation: The pellicle is a flexible but firm layer that keeps the slipper shape of Paramecium.

questions.stem: Cycads and conifers belong to the group
questions.explanation: They are seed plants whose seeds are borne naked on cones.

questions.stem: The body wall of Hydra is described as diploblastic because it
options: is made of a single cell
has two layers of cells separated by a jelly-like mesogloea
questions.explanation: Hydra has an ectoderm and an endoderm but no true mesoderm.

questions.stem: Hydra captures its prey with the help of
questions.explanation: Cnidoblasts fire threads that paralyse small animals, which the tentacles then push into the mouth.

questions.stem: Humans usually become infected with the pork tapeworm, Taenia solium, by
options: drinking water contaminated with its eggs only
eating undercooked pork that contains bladderworms (cysticerci)
questions.explanation: Thorough cooking kills the larval cysts in pork muscle.

questions.stem: An adult tapeworm has no alimentary canal because it
options: absorbs already-digested food through its body surface
questions.explanation: It lives in the host's intestine, surrounded by digested food.

questions.stem: Roundworms (Nematoda) differ from flatworms (Platyhelminthes) in having
options: a body made of two cell layers only
a complete gut with both a mouth and an anus
questions.explanation: Flatworms have a gut with only one opening, or no gut at all, as in tapeworms.

questions.stem: Which of these organisms is a nematode (roundworm)?
questions.explanation: Ascaris is a roundworm that lives in the human intestine. Taenia is a flatworm and the earthworm is an annelid.

questions.stem: The earthworm belongs to the phylum
questions.explanation: Annelids are segmented worms.

questions.stem: The clitellum of an earthworm
options: is the brain of the worm
secretes the cocoon in which the eggs develop
questions.explanation: The clitellum is the thickened band of segments that forms the cocoon during reproduction.

questions.stem: An earthworm carries out gaseous exchange through its
questions.explanation: The thin, moist skin, which has many blood capillaries, is its respiratory surface.

questions.stem: Which pair of features is shared by all arthropods?
options: Jointed appendages and an exoskeleton made of chitin
Soft unsegmented bodies and a shell
questions.explanation: Arthropod means "jointed foot". The chitin exoskeleton has to be moulted for the animal to grow.

questions.stem: An adult insect has
options: four pairs of legs and a body divided into two parts
many pairs of legs, one on each segment
three pairs of legs and a body divided into head, thorax and abdomen
no legs and an unsegmented body
questions.explanation: Six legs and three body regions are the distinguishing features of insects.

questions.stem: A spider differs from an insect in having
options: three pairs of legs and wings
four pairs of legs and a body in two parts
questions.explanation: Spiders are arachnids. They have eight legs, no antennae and a cephalothorax joined to an abdomen.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the life cycle of a housefly?
questions.explanation: The housefly undergoes complete metamorphosis. Its larva is called a maggot.

questions.stem: The cockroach shows incomplete metamorphosis, which means its life cycle is
questions.explanation: Nymphs look like small, wingless adults and moult several times as they grow.

questions.stem: The land snail belongs to the phylum
questions.explanation: Molluscs have soft, unsegmented bodies, a muscular foot and usually a shell.

questions.stem: Which of these is a cartilaginous fish?
questions.explanation: Sharks and rays have skeletons made of cartilage. The others are bony fish.

questions.stem: The lateral line of a fish is used to
options: detect vibrations and pressure changes in the water
questions.explanation: It is a sense organ running along each side of the body.

questions.stem: Frogs and toads are able to exchange gases through their skin because the skin is
options: thin, moist and well supplied with blood vessels
questions.explanation: Amphibians use both lungs and skin for gaseous exchange.

questions.stem: Reptiles are better adapted to life on land than amphibians partly because reptiles
options: lay eggs with leathery shells on land
questions.explanation: Shelled eggs do not dry out, so reptiles do not need water for reproduction.

questions.stem: Which feature is found only in birds?
questions.explanation: Bats and insects also have wings, and some reptiles lay eggs, but only birds have feathers.

questions.stem: Which two features are found only in mammals?
questions.explanation: Mammals have hair and suckle their young with milk.

questions.stem: The bat is classified as a mammal and not a bird because it
options: has fur and suckles its young
questions.explanation: Flight is not a feature of mammals as such. Hair and milk are what make the bat a mammal.

questions.stem: A whale lives in the sea, yet it is classified as a mammal because it
options: breathes air with lungs and suckles its young
questions.explanation: Whales are warm-blooded, breathe with lungs, give birth to live young and feed them on milk.

questions.stem: An animal has a segmented body, a closed blood system, a moist skin used for breathing, and each individual has both male and female organs. The animal is most likely
questions.explanation: Annelids such as the earthworm have all these features. Cockroaches have an open blood system and separate sexes.

questions.stem: Which group of vertebrates is poikilothermic (cold-blooded)?
questions.explanation: Their body temperature changes with the temperature of their surroundings. Birds and mammals are homoiothermic.

questions.stem: The larva of the Culex mosquito obtains air by
options: hanging from the water surface and breathing through a siphon (breathing tube)
questions.explanation: The siphon at the tail end of the larva pierces the surface film to reach the air.

questions.stem: The female Anopheles mosquito transmits
questions.explanation: Plasmodium is passed to humans in the saliva of the female mosquito when she takes a blood meal.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: The mouthparts of the female mosquito are adapted for
options: sucking nectar from deep flowers through a coiled tube
piercing the skin and sucking blood
questions.explanation: Its needle-like stylets pierce the skin, and blood is sucked up through a food channel.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: The long proboscis of a butterfly is adapted for
options: sucking nectar from flowers, and it is coiled up when not in use
questions.explanation: A long tube lets the butterfly reach nectar deep inside a flower.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: The housefly feeds using mouthparts adapted for
options: sponging and sucking up liquid food
questions.explanation: The fly pours saliva onto its food and mops up the dissolved food with the spongy pads of its proboscis.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: The strong hooked beak of an eagle is adapted for
questions.explanation: Birds of prey use their hooked beaks to tear meat. Seed-eaters have short, stout beaks.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: The webbed feet of a duck are adapted for
questions.explanation: The web of skin between the toes pushes against the water like a paddle.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: The stick insect escapes from predators mainly by
options: camouflage, because its body looks like a twig
questions.explanation: Predators fail to notice it among the twigs of a plant.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: Many fishes and antelopes are dark on the upper side and pale on the underside. This counter-shading
options: makes them harder for predators to see
warns predators that they are poisonous
questions.explanation: Light from above makes the dark back look paler and the shaded pale belly look darker, so the animal looks flat and blends into the background.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: Brightly coloured poisonous animals, such as some frogs and caterpillars, show warning colouration. This colouration
options: tells predators that the animal is harmful or tastes bad
questions.explanation: Predators learn to avoid the bright pattern after a bad experience.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: The bright red head of the adult male Agama lizard helps it to
options: attract females and warn off rival males
questions.explanation: This is an adaptation for securing mates and defending territory. Females and young males are dull brown.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: A toad protects itself from many predators by
options: releasing distasteful or poisonous substances from glands in its skin
questions.explanation: Its skin glands (the parotoid glands) make the toad unpleasant to eat.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: The display of colourful tail feathers by a male peacock is a behavioural adaptation for
questions.explanation: Females choose males with the most impressive displays.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: In cacti, the leaves are reduced to spines. This mainly helps the plant to
questions.explanation: Spines have a very small surface area. The green stem takes over photosynthesis.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: In a colony of honey bees, the workers
options: collect food, build the comb, look after the young and defend the hive
questions.explanation: Workers are sterile females. The queen lays the eggs and the drones mate with her.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: In a termite colony, the reproductive caste is made up of the
questions.explanation: Only the royal pair reproduces. Soldiers defend the colony and workers build and gather food.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: On a cold morning, birds fluff up their feathers. This helps them to
options: trap a layer of air, which insulates the body
questions.explanation: Still air is a poor conductor of heat, so less body heat is lost.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: The large, spiny front legs of the praying mantis are adapted for
questions.explanation: The mantis waits motionless and then snaps up insects with its forelegs.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: In many xerophytes, the stomata are sunken in pits on the leaf surface. This
questions.explanation: Humid air trapped in the pits lowers the diffusion gradient for water vapour.

questions.topic: Structural, functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
questions.stem: A harmless hoverfly has black and yellow stripes like a wasp. The advantage to the hoverfly is that
options: it can sting like a wasp
predators that have learnt to avoid stinging wasps also avoid the hoverfly
questions.explanation: This is mimicry. The harmless mimic benefits from the warning colouration of the harmful model.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: In a transverse section of a young dicotyledonous stem, the vascular bundles are arranged
questions.explanation: Monocot stems, such as maize, have scattered vascular bundles.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: In the stem of a monocotyledon such as maize, the vascular bundles are
questions.explanation: This scattered arrangement is a typical monocot feature.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: In the young root of a dicotyledon, the xylem and phloem are arranged
options: in a ring of separate bundles, with phloem outside xylem on the same radius
on alternate radii, with the xylem often forming a star shape in the centre
questions.explanation: In roots, xylem and phloem lie on alternate radii. In stems they lie on the same radius in each bundle.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: The vascular cambium of a dicot stem is responsible for
questions.explanation: The cambium divides to form new xylem towards the inside and new phloem towards the outside.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: The endodermis of a root, with its Casparian strip,
options: controls the passage of water and minerals into the vascular tissue
questions.explanation: The waterproof Casparian strip forces water to pass through living endodermal cells, which select what enters.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: Most chloroplasts in a leaf are found in the palisade layer because this layer
options: is next to the lower epidermis
lies just below the upper epidermis, where it receives the most light
questions.explanation: Its tightly packed, column-shaped cells are placed to absorb as much light as possible.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: The large air spaces in the spongy mesophyll of a leaf
options: allow gases to diffuse to and from the cells
questions.explanation: CO2 and O2 move between the stomata and the mesophyll cells through the air spaces.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: The waxy cuticle on the upper surface of a leaf
questions.explanation: The waxy layer is waterproof, so less water evaporates from the leaf surface.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: In a mammal, the thoracic cavity is separated from the abdominal cavity by the
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle that also helps in breathing.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: Which group of organs lies in the abdominal cavity of a mammal?
questions.explanation: The heart and lungs are in the thorax. The digestive and excretory organs are in the abdomen.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: In roots, lateral (branch) roots arise from the
questions.explanation: Pericycle cells divide and the new root pushes out through the cortex.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: Root hairs, which grow from the piliferous layer of a young root,
options: increase the surface area for absorbing water and mineral salts
questions.explanation: Each root hair is a long, thin outgrowth of an epidermal cell.

questions.topic: Internal structure of plants and animals
questions.stem: In phloem tissue, the cells closely associated with the sieve tubes and which control their activities are the
questions.explanation: Sieve tube elements have no nucleus, so the companion cells next to them keep them alive and working.

questions.stem: Organisms that make their own food from simple inorganic substances are called
questions.explanation: Green plants (photosynthesis) and some bacteria (chemosynthesis) are autotrophs.

questions.stem: Chemosynthetic bacteria get the energy they need to make food from
options: the oxidation of inorganic substances such as ammonia or hydrogen sulphide
questions.explanation: Nitrifying bacteria, for example, oxidise ammonium compounds and use the energy released to fix carbon.

questions.stem: What are the raw materials for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 in the presence of light and chlorophyll.

questions.stem: The oxygen given off by green plants during photosynthesis comes from
questions.explanation: In the light stage, water is split (photolysis), which releases oxygen. The carbon in CO2 ends up in sugar.

questions.stem: The light-dependent stage of photosynthesis takes place in the
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll in the grana traps light energy. Carbon fixation takes place in the stroma.

questions.stem: Which products of the light stage of photosynthesis are used in the light-independent (dark) stage?
questions.explanation: ATP provides energy and reduced NADP provides hydrogen for reducing CO2 to sugar.

questions.stem: Before an experiment to show that light is needed for photosynthesis, a potted plant is kept in darkness for about 48 hours in order to
options: remove the starch already present in its leaves (destarch it)
questions.explanation: Any starch found at the end must then have been made during the experiment.

questions.stem: When a leaf is tested for starch, it is boiled in alcohol (ethanol) in order to
options: soften the cuticle so that iodine can enter
remove the chlorophyll so that the colour change can be seen
questions.explanation: Green chlorophyll would hide the blue-black colour. The earlier dip in boiling water kills and softens the cells.

questions.stem: A variegated leaf (green and white) is tested for starch after being kept in light. Only the parts that were green turn blue-black. This shows that
options: carbon(IV) oxide is necessary for photosynthesis
oxygen is given off during photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Both parts of the leaf had light and CO2. Only the parts with chlorophyll made starch.

questions.stem: In an experiment, one leaf of a destarched plant is enclosed in a flask containing potassium hydroxide solution, and the plant is left in light. This experiment tests the need for
questions.explanation: KOH absorbs CO2. The leaf in the flask makes no starch.

questions.stem: Which of these elements is a macronutrient for plants?
questions.explanation: Macronutrients (N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S) are needed in large amounts. Zinc, copper and boron are micronutrients (trace elements).

questions.stem: Which of these elements is a micronutrient (trace element) for plants?
questions.explanation: Manganese is needed only in very small amounts, mainly for enzyme activity.

questions.stem: Magnesium is essential for green plants mainly because it
options: is part of the chlorophyll molecule
is needed to make cell walls
questions.explanation: Without magnesium, plants cannot make chlorophyll and their leaves turn yellow (chlorosis).

questions.stem: Plants need nitrogen mainly for making
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is part of every amino acid. Plants deficient in it are stunted and pale.

questions.stem: Which reagent is used to test a food sample for reducing sugars?
questions.explanation: On heating, a reducing sugar turns blue Benedict's solution green, yellow, orange or brick red.

questions.stem: Rubbing a food sample on paper leaves a translucent (greasy) spot that does not dry out. This shows that the food contains
questions.explanation: Fats stain paper permanently. A spot of water dries up.

questions.stem: When Sudan III solution is shaken with a food sample in water, a red-stained layer forms on top. This shows the presence of
questions.explanation: Sudan III dissolves in lipids, and the stained lipid floats on the water.

questions.stem: Millon's reagent is used to test for
questions.explanation: On warming, proteins give a brick-red or pink precipitate with Millon's reagent.

questions.stem: Rickets, in which children develop soft, bent leg bones, is caused by a lack of
questions.explanation: Vitamin D is needed to absorb the calcium that hardens bones. It is made in the skin in sunlight.

questions.stem: Scurvy, with bleeding gums and slow healing of wounds, is caused by a lack of
questions.explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is found in fresh fruits such as oranges and in vegetables.

questions.stem: Night blindness is caused by a lack of
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is needed to make the light-sensitive pigment in the rod cells of the retina. Palm oil and carrots are good sources.

questions.stem: Beriberi, which affects the nerves and muscles, is caused by a shortage of
questions.explanation: It is common where people eat mainly polished rice, because the thiamine-rich husk is removed.

questions.stem: Kwashiorkor in young children is caused mainly by a diet that is low in
questions.explanation: Signs include a swollen belly (oedema), changes in hair colour and poor growth, often after weaning onto a starchy diet.

questions.stem: A lack of iron in the diet leads to
questions.explanation: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin. Too little iron means fewer red blood cells and tiredness.

questions.stem: A swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck (goitre) is caused by a lack of
questions.explanation: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine. Iodised salt helps to prevent goitre.

questions.stem: Roughage (dietary fibre) is important in the diet because it
questions.explanation: Humans cannot digest cellulose, but its bulk helps the gut muscles to push food along.

questions.stem: Which teeth are used mainly for grinding and crushing food?
questions.explanation: Molars have broad, ridged surfaces. Incisors cut and canines tear.

questions.stem: Long, pointed canine teeth are best developed in
questions.explanation: Carnivores use their canines to grip and kill prey and to tear flesh.

questions.stem: In herbivores such as goats, the diastema (a gap between the front teeth and the cheek teeth)
options: lets the tongue move grass about before it is ground
is a sign of tooth decay
questions.explanation: Herbivores have no canines, or very small ones, and the gap lets the tongue move food to the grinding teeth.

questions.stem: A child's milk (deciduous) dentition has the dental formula i 2/2, c 1/1, m 2/2. How many teeth does the child have in total?
questions.explanation: Teeth on one side = (2 + 1 + 2) upper + (2 + 1 + 2) lower = 10. Doubling for both sides gives 20.

questions.stem: A mammal has the dental formula i 0/3, c 0/1, pm 3/3, m 3/3. How many teeth does it have in total, and what kind of mammal is it most likely to be?
options: 32; a ruminant herbivore such as a cow
32; a carnivore such as a dog
44; an omnivore such as a pig
20; a rodent such as a rat
questions.explanation: Total = 2 x [(0 + 0 + 3 + 3) + (3 + 1 + 3 + 3)] = 2 x 16 = 32. With no upper incisors (there is a horny pad instead), it is a ruminant.

questions.stem: The hardest substance in the mammalian body is
questions.explanation: Enamel covers the crown of each tooth and protects it from wear.

questions.stem: The pulp cavity of a tooth contains
questions.explanation: The blood vessels nourish the tooth, and the nerves make it sensitive.

questions.stem: Saliva contains the enzyme salivary amylase (ptyalin), which
options: begins the digestion of cooked starch to maltose
questions.explanation: Starch digestion starts in the mouth, in slightly alkaline conditions.

questions.stem: Pepsin works best in the
options: alkaline conditions of the mouth, where it digests starch
small intestine, where it digests fats
large intestine, where it absorbs water
acidic conditions of the stomach, where it begins the digestion of proteins
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach gives the low pH that pepsin needs.

questions.stem: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the
questions.explanation: Bile enters the duodenum through the bile duct and emulsifies fats.

questions.stem: Bile salts help digestion by
options: emulsifying fats into tiny droplets, which increases the surface area for lipase
questions.explanation: Bile contains no enzymes, but emulsification speeds up the digestion of fat.

questions.stem: The villi of the small intestine are adapted for absorption because they
options: greatly increase the surface area and have a rich blood supply
questions.explanation: Millions of finger-like villi, each with capillaries and a lacteal, make absorption fast.

questions.stem: The lacteal in each villus absorbs mainly
questions.explanation: Products of fat digestion pass into the lymphatic system through the lacteals.

questions.stem: The hydrochloric acid secreted in the stomach
options: kills many bacteria and gives the acidic conditions that pepsin needs
questions.explanation: The low pH also helps to activate pepsinogen into pepsin.

questions.stem: In young mammals, the enzyme rennin
options: breaks down fats in the duodenum
curdles (coagulates) milk protein in the stomach
questions.explanation: Curdled milk stays longer in the stomach, which gives pepsin time to digest it.

questions.stem: Most digested food is absorbed into the blood in the
questions.explanation: The ileum is long and lined with villi.

questions.stem: The main function of the colon (large intestine) is to
questions.explanation: Water is absorbed, so the waste becomes semi-solid faeces.

questions.stem: Assimilation is
options: the intake of food through the mouth
the breakdown of large food molecules
the use of absorbed food substances by body cells
questions.explanation: For example, amino acids are built into new proteins and glucose is used in respiration.

questions.stem: Saliva was boiled, cooled and added to starch solution. After 30 minutes at 37 °C, the mixture still gave a blue-black colour with iodine. This is because
questions.explanation: High temperature permanently changes the shape of the enzyme's active site, so the starch was not digested.

questions.stem: Ruminants such as cows are able to digest cellulose because
options: their teeth grind cellulose to glucose
micro-organisms in the rumen produce cellulase
questions.explanation: Mammals do not make cellulase themselves. The bacteria in the rumen do the digestion for them.

questions.stem: Insectivorous plants such as the pitcher plant trap and digest insects mainly to obtain
questions.explanation: They grow in nitrogen-poor soils and get nitrogen from the bodies of the insects.

questions.stem: Dodder (Cuscuta), a parasitic flowering plant, obtains food from its host by means of
options: haustoria that grow into the host's phloem
questions.explanation: Haustoria are special suckers that draw food out of the host's vascular tissue.

questions.stem: Holozoic nutrition involves
options: making food from carbon(IV) oxide and water
taking in solid food, then digesting, absorbing and assimilating it
absorbing digested food from a dead body
living inside a host and absorbing its food
questions.explanation: Most animals, including humans, feed holozoically.

questions.stem: Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests proteins?
questions.explanation: Trypsin digests proteins in the alkaline conditions of the duodenum. Amylase and lipase digest starch and fats.

questions.stem: Large multicellular organisms need a transport system mainly because
options: their cells are all on the surface
their surface area to volume ratio is small, so diffusion alone is too slow to reach all cells
questions.explanation: In a large body, most cells are far from the surface, so materials must be carried to them.

questions.stem: Diffusion is the
options: movement of water only across a membrane
movement of particles against a concentration gradient using energy
net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration
questions.explanation: Diffusion is passive and continues until the concentrations are equal.

questions.stem: Osmosis is the movement of
options: water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution
solute particles from a concentrated to a dilute solution
any particles from low to high concentration using energy
questions.explanation: Water moves from where its concentration is higher (the dilute solution) to where it is lower.

questions.stem: Red blood cells placed in distilled water
options: shrink, because water leaves them by osmosis
swell and burst, because water enters them by osmosis
questions.explanation: Animal cells have no cell wall to stop them bursting (haemolysis).

questions.stem: When a plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution, its cytoplasm shrinks away from the cell wall. This is called
questions.explanation: The cell loses water by osmosis, and the cell wall keeps its shape while the protoplast shrinks.

questions.stem: Active transport differs from diffusion because active transport
options: moves substances against a concentration gradient and uses energy from respiration
questions.explanation: Root hair cells take up mineral ions from dilute soil water by active transport.

questions.stem: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are called
questions.explanation: Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand high pressure.

questions.stem: The pulmonary vein carries
options: oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium
deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs
oxygenated blood from the heart to the body
deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium
questions.explanation: It is the only vein that carries oxygenated blood. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.

questions.stem: Which chamber of the mammalian heart has the thickest muscular wall?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps blood through the whole body, so it needs to produce the most force.

questions.stem: The valves in veins
questions.explanation: Blood pressure in veins is low, so the valves make sure that blood flows only towards the heart.

questions.stem: Capillary walls are only one cell thick. This allows
options: blood to flow at high pressure
easy exchange of materials between blood and tissue cells
questions.explanation: A short diffusion distance makes exchange fast.

questions.stem: Absorbed glucose and amino acids are carried from the small intestine to the liver in the
questions.explanation: This lets the liver process the digested food before it reaches the rest of the body.

questions.stem: Mammals are said to have a double circulation because
options: blood flows in two directions in each vessel
they have both arteries and veins
blood passes through the heart twice during one complete circuit of the body
questions.explanation: There is a pulmonary circuit (heart to lungs to heart) and a systemic circuit (heart to body to heart).

questions.stem: Mature mammalian red blood cells have no nucleus. This
options: leaves more space for haemoglobin to carry oxygen
questions.explanation: Their biconcave shape and lack of a nucleus both help them carry as much oxygen as possible.

questions.stem: Which component of blood helps in clotting?
questions.explanation: Platelets release substances that start the chain of reactions forming a fibrin clot.

questions.stem: Phagocytes are white blood cells that protect the body by
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes produce antibodies, and phagocytes engulf micro-organisms.

questions.stem: Which of these substances is carried mainly dissolved in blood plasma?
questions.explanation: Plasma carries dissolved food, urea, hormones and most CO2 (as hydrogencarbonate). Most oxygen is carried by red cells.

questions.stem: Lymph from most of the body returns to the bloodstream through the
options: thoracic duct, which empties into a large vein near the heart
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct joins the left subclavian vein, returning tissue fluid to the blood.

questions.stem: In flowering plants, water and mineral salts are carried from the roots to the leaves in the
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes strengthened with lignin.

questions.stem: Food made in the leaves (mainly sucrose) is carried to other parts of the plant in the
questions.explanation: The movement of food in the phloem is called translocation.

questions.stem: A ring of bark (including the phloem) is removed from the stem of a woody plant. After some weeks, the bark just above the ring swells. This shows that
options: food made in the leaves moves down the stem in the phloem
water moves up the stem in the phloem
questions.explanation: Food moving downwards builds up above the cut. Water still rises because the xylem is not removed.

questions.stem: The main force that draws water up the xylem of a tall tree is
options: transpiration pull, caused by evaporation of water from the leaves
questions.explanation: Water lost from the leaves pulls up an unbroken column of water held together by cohesion.

questions.stem: A potometer is used to measure the
options: rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot
questions.explanation: The water taken up is roughly equal to the water lost in transpiration.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions would give the highest rate of transpiration?
questions.explanation: Heat, low humidity and wind all increase the gradient of water vapour between the leaf and the air.

questions.stem: When the stem of a well-watered plant is cut off near ground level, sap oozes from the cut stump. This is evidence of
questions.explanation: Roots actively take up ions, so water follows by osmosis and is pushed up the xylem.

questions.stem: The tricuspid valve is found between the
questions.explanation: The bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the left side of the heart.

questions.stem: The sino-atrial node (pacemaker) in the right atrium
options: starts each heartbeat by sending out electrical impulses
questions.explanation: The impulse spreads over the atria and then to the ventricles, making them contract.

questions.stem: In the lungs, haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form
questions.explanation: Oxyhaemoglobin releases oxygen in the tissues, where the oxygen concentration is low.

questions.stem: Which word equation summarises aerobic respiration?
options: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon(IV) oxide + water + energy
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely, using oxygen.

questions.stem: In which part of the cell does glycolysis take place?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis splits glucose into two molecules of pyruvate in the cytoplasm, and needs no oxygen.

questions.stem: The Krebs (citric acid) cycle takes place in the
questions.explanation: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, where it is fully oxidised to CO2.

questions.stem: During vigorous exercise, human muscle cells short of oxygen respire anaerobically and produce
questions.explanation: A build-up of lactic acid leads to muscle fatigue.

questions.stem: When yeast respires without oxygen, it produces
questions.explanation: This alcoholic fermentation is used in brewing and baking.

questions.stem: In the textbook account, about how many molecules of ATP are produced from the complete aerobic respiration of one molecule of glucose?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain together give a maximum of about 38 ATP, compared with 2 from anaerobic respiration.

questions.stem: The net gain of ATP when one molecule of glucose is respired anaerobically is
questions.explanation: Only glycolysis takes place, so very little of the energy in glucose is released.

questions.stem: The oxygen debt after a short race is
options: the oxygen used before the race
carbon(IV) oxide breathed out during the race
the extra oxygen needed afterwards to break down the lactic acid built up during the race
questions.explanation: This is why you continue to breathe deeply after strenuous exercise has stopped.

questions.stem: Which set of features is typical of an efficient respiratory surface?
options: Thick, dry and small in area
Thin, moist, large in area and with a good blood supply
Thin, dry and with no blood supply
Thick, moist and with a poor blood supply
questions.explanation: These features allow fast diffusion of oxygen and carbon(IV) oxide.

questions.stem: Insects carry out gaseous exchange through
options: a system of tracheae that open to the air through spiracles
questions.explanation: Air tubes carry oxygen directly to the tissues, so blood is not needed for transporting gases.

questions.stem: In a bony fish, gaseous exchange takes place as
options: water flows over the gill filaments in the opposite direction to the blood flowing through them
air is swallowed into the lungs
water is absorbed through the skin
water passes through the swim bladder
questions.explanation: This counter-current flow keeps a diffusion gradient along the whole length of the filament.

questions.stem: During inspiration (breathing in) in a mammal,
options: the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped
the ribs move downwards and inwards
the volume of the thorax decreases
the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs
questions.explanation: The volume of the thorax increases and the pressure inside it falls, so air rushes into the lungs.

questions.stem: In flowering plants, gases are exchanged with the air mainly through
options: stomata in the leaves and lenticels in woody stems
questions.explanation: Lenticels are loosely packed areas in bark that allow gas exchange.

questions.stem: Germinating seeds gave out 20 cm^3 of carbon(IV) oxide while taking in 28 cm^3 of oxygen. Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ = CO2 given out / O2 taken in). Which food is mainly being respired?
questions.explanation: RQ = 20/28 = 0.71. This is the typical value for fats, whereas carbohydrates give about 1.0. Oil-rich seeds such as groundnut give values like this.

questions.stem: Air breathed out is bubbled through one tube of lime water, and room air is drawn through another. The lime water in the first tube turns milky faster. This shows that
options: inhaled air contains no carbon(IV) oxide
exhaled air contains more carbon(IV) oxide than inhaled air
questions.explanation: CO2 produced in respiration is breathed out, so exhaled air has a higher CO2 concentration.

questions.stem: Alveoli are well adapted for gaseous exchange because they
options: have very thin, moist walls surrounded by a dense network of capillaries
questions.explanation: Millions of alveoli give a huge surface area and a short diffusion distance.

questions.stem: Germinating seeds in a vacuum flask show a rise in temperature over a few days because
options: respiration in the seeds releases energy as heat
the seeds absorb heat from the air
questions.explanation: The control flask contains boiled (dead) seeds, which show no rise in temperature.

questions.stem: ATP is described as the energy currency of the cell because it
options: is a type of sugar used for storage
stores energy released in respiration and releases it where the cell needs it
questions.explanation: ATP is broken down to ADP to power processes such as muscle contraction and active transport.

questions.stem: The C-shaped rings of cartilage in the trachea
options: keep the airway open during breathing
questions.explanation: The cartilage stops the trachea collapsing when the pressure inside it falls.

questions.stem: The mucus and cilia that line the trachea and bronchi
options: trap dust and germs and sweep them up towards the throat
questions.explanation: This cleans the incoming air. Cigarette smoke damages the cilia.

questions.stem: A young tadpole takes in oxygen from the water mainly through its
questions.explanation: Tadpoles first have external gills, then internal gills. Adult frogs use lungs and skin.

questions.stem: The contractile vacuole of Amoeba
options: removes excess water that enters the cell by osmosis
questions.explanation: Freshwater protozoa constantly take in water. The vacuole fills and empties to stop the cell bursting.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches an organism with its excretory structure?
questions.explanation: Flatworms have flame cells, insects have Malpighian tubules, and Amoeba uses its cell membrane and contractile vacuole.

questions.stem: Insects excrete their nitrogenous waste mainly as
options: urea dissolved in a lot of water
questions.explanation: Uric acid is almost insoluble, so it can be excreted with very little loss of water, which suits life on land.

questions.stem: The functional unit of the mammalian kidney is the
questions.explanation: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, which filter blood and form urine.

questions.stem: Ultrafiltration of blood in the kidney takes place in the
questions.explanation: High blood pressure in the glomerulus forces water and small solutes into the capsule.

questions.stem: In a healthy person, all the glucose in the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed into the blood in the
questions.explanation: This happens by active transport, so normal urine contains no glucose.

questions.stem: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) causes
options: more water to be reabsorbed from the collecting ducts, so less urine is produced
questions.explanation: ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water. It is released when the body is short of water.

questions.stem: Urea is formed in the
options: liver, from the breakdown of excess amino acids (deamination)
questions.explanation: The amino groups are converted to urea, which is carried by the blood to the kidneys.

questions.stem: Laboratory tests show glucose in a patient's urine. This most likely indicates
questions.explanation: Without enough insulin, blood glucose rises so high that the kidney tubules cannot reabsorb it all.

questions.stem: Apart from oxygen, the lungs excrete
questions.explanation: These waste products of respiration are breathed out.

questions.stem: The skin acts as an excretory organ because sweat removes
options: water, salts and a small amount of urea
questions.explanation: The main function of sweating is cooling, but it also gets rid of some waste.

questions.stem: Which of these are excretory products of plants?
questions.explanation: Plants store some wastes in the bark, leaves and other tissues and get rid of them when these are shed.

questions.stem: Plants get rid of the gaseous waste products of metabolism mainly through
questions.explanation: Plants have no special excretory organs. Gases diffuse out through these pores.

questions.stem: The glomerular filtrate normally contains no
questions.explanation: These are too large to pass through the filtration barrier.

questions.stem: The ureter carries urine from the
questions.explanation: The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside.

questions.stem: Most bony freshwater fishes excrete their nitrogenous waste as ammonia because
options: they cannot make urea or uric acid because they lack a liver
ammonia is very soluble and toxic, but it is quickly diluted and carried away by the water around them
questions.explanation: Getting rid of ammonia needs a lot of water. Freshwater fishes have plenty of water, so they do not need to spend energy turning it into urea.

questions.stem: A tropism is
options: the movement of a whole organism from place to place in response to a stimulus
a movement of a plant part that does not depend on the direction of the stimulus
the folding of leaves at night
a growth movement of part of a plant in response to a stimulus coming from one direction
questions.explanation: Tropisms are directional growth responses, such as bending towards light.

questions.stem: A seedling on a windowsill bends towards the window. This response is called
questions.explanation: The shoot grows towards light coming from one side.

questions.stem: The main root of a seedling grows downwards whichever way the seed is planted. This is
questions.explanation: Roots grow towards the pull of gravity, and shoots grow away from it.

questions.stem: When a shoot is lit from one side, it bends towards the light because
options: auxin collects on the shaded side and makes those cells grow longer
auxin collects on the lit side and makes those cells grow longer
light kills the cells on the shaded side
cells on the lit side take in more water
questions.explanation: Uneven growth on the two sides makes the shoot curve towards the light.

questions.stem: Euglena swims towards a source of light. This type of response is called
questions.explanation: In a tactic movement the whole organism moves towards or away from a directional stimulus.

questions.stem: The leaflets of the sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica) fold up quickly when touched. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Nastic movements do not depend on the direction of the stimulus. They are caused by changes in turgor.

questions.stem: The leaves of some legumes fold up at night and open again in the morning. This is called
questions.explanation: This daily rhythm of folding is a nastic response to changes in light and temperature.

questions.stem: In tropism experiments, a klinostat is used to
options: rotate a seedling slowly so that a one-sided stimulus such as gravity acts equally on all sides
questions.explanation: A seedling on a rotating klinostat grows straight, which serves as a control.

questions.stem: A tendril coils around a support because of
questions.explanation: Cells on the side away from the contact grow faster, so the tendril curls around the support.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of an exoskeleton, as found in insects, is that it
options: has to be shed (moulted) before the animal can grow larger
questions.explanation: The hard chitin covering cannot stretch, so arthropods moult, and they are vulnerable until the new covering hardens.

questions.stem: The endoskeleton of a mammal is made mainly of
questions.explanation: Bone gives rigid support, and cartilage covers the joints and supports structures such as the ear.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a job of the bones of a mammal?
questions.explanation: The skeleton supports and protects the body, allows movement and makes blood cells in the marrow, but it does not digest food.

questions.stem: The shoulder joint is an example of
questions.explanation: The head of the humerus fits into the glenoid cavity, which allows movement in many directions.

questions.stem: The elbow joint is an example of
questions.explanation: A hinge joint allows movement in one plane only, like a door hinge.

questions.stem: Ligaments are tough, slightly elastic tissues that join
options: bone to bone at a joint
questions.explanation: Ligaments hold the bones of a joint together. Tendons attach muscles to bones.

questions.stem: Tendons are strong, non-elastic tissues that join
questions.explanation: Because they do not stretch, all the pull of a contracting muscle is passed to the bone.

questions.stem: The synovial fluid in a movable joint
options: lubricates the joint and reduces friction
questions.explanation: It is secreted by the synovial membrane and keeps the cartilage surfaces moving smoothly.

questions.stem: When the biceps muscle contracts,
options: the triceps also contracts and the arm straightens
the triceps relaxes and the arm bends at the elbow
questions.explanation: The biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair: when one contracts, the other relaxes.

questions.stem: Which vertebrae have the largest centra and short, thick neural spines, suited to bearing the weight of the upper body?
questions.explanation: Lumbar vertebrae in the lower back carry heavy loads and give attachment to large back muscles.

questions.stem: Thoracic vertebrae can be recognised by
options: their fusion to form a single bone
the facets on which the ribs articulate
questions.explanation: The ribs attach to the thoracic vertebrae, forming the rib cage. Vertebrarterial canals are found in cervical vertebrae.

questions.stem: Young herbaceous (non-woody) plants are supported mainly by
questions.explanation: When the cells lose water, these plants wilt.

questions.stem: The earthworm has no bones. Its body is supported by
options: a hydrostatic skeleton of fluid under pressure in the body cavity
questions.explanation: The muscles of the body wall push against the fluid-filled coelom.

questions.stem: Bone is hard mainly because it contains
questions.explanation: Mineral salts give bone its hardness, and the protein collagen gives it some flexibility.

questions.stem: The head of the humerus fits into the glenoid cavity of the
questions.explanation: The scapula (shoulder blade) is part of the pectoral girdle.

questions.stem: The head of the femur fits into a socket in the pelvic girdle called the
questions.explanation: The acetabulum and the femur form the ball-and-socket joint of the hip.

questions.stem: In woody plants, the tissues that give mechanical support are mainly
options: xylem and sclerenchyma, whose cell walls are thickened with lignin
questions.explanation: Lignin is a hard, rigid substance that strengthens wood.

questions.stem: Paramecium reproduces asexually by
questions.explanation: The single cell divides into two similar daughter cells.

questions.stem: Yeast commonly reproduces asexually by
questions.explanation: A small outgrowth forms on the parent cell, gets bigger and then separates.

questions.stem: Farmers in Nigeria usually propagate cassava from
questions.explanation: Pieces of mature stem planted in the soil grow roots and shoots.

questions.stem: Bryophyllum reproduces vegetatively by means of
options: buds that grow into new plantlets along the edges of its leaves
questions.explanation: The plantlets drop off and take root.

questions.stem: In grafting, the scion is
options: the rooted plant that receives the graft
the tape used to bind the graft
the shoot or bud of the desired variety that is joined onto a rooted plant
a seed planted beside the stock
questions.explanation: The rooted part is the stock. Grafting is widely used for oranges and mangoes.

questions.stem: An advantage of vegetative propagation to farmers is that
options: it produces a lot of variation
the offspring are identical to the parent, so useful features are kept
the plants can be spread over long distances by wind
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction keeps desirable features such as high yield exactly the same.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of asexual reproduction is that
options: the offspring show little variation, so one disease can wipe them all out
questions.explanation: Genetically identical plants are all equally vulnerable to the same pest or disease.

questions.stem: In a flower, pollen grains are produced in the
questions.explanation: The anther and filament together make up the stamen.

questions.stem: The part of the flower that receives pollen grains during pollination is the
questions.explanation: The stigma is often sticky or feathery so that pollen sticks to it.

questions.stem: Which set of features is typical of insect-pollinated flowers?
options: Brightly coloured petals, scent, nectar and sticky pollen
Feathery stigmas, small dull petals and light, smooth pollen
No petals and anthers hanging outside the flower
Large amounts of very light pollen and no nectar
questions.explanation: These features attract insects and make the pollen stick to their bodies.

questions.stem: Which feature is typical of a wind-pollinated flower such as grass or maize?
options: Large, feathery stigmas that hang outside the flower
questions.explanation: Feathery stigmas give a large surface for catching airborne pollen.

questions.stem: Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen from
options: a flower on one plant to a flower on a different plant of the same species
an anther to a stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant
questions.explanation: Cross-pollination is between different plants of the same species.

questions.stem: In some flowers the anthers ripen before the stigma of the same flower is ready (protandry). This
questions.explanation: Because the stigma is not receptive when its own pollen is released, it is likely to receive pollen from another flower.

questions.stem: In the double fertilisation of flowering plants, one male nucleus fuses with the egg cell, and the other fuses with
options: the two polar nuclei, forming the triploid endosperm nucleus
the antipodal cells, forming the testa
the pollen tube nucleus, forming the radicle
questions.explanation: The fertilised egg forms the diploid embryo, and the triploid endosperm stores food.

questions.stem: After fertilisation in a flowering plant, the ovary develops into the
questions.explanation: The ovules become seeds, and the ovary wall becomes the wall of the fruit (pericarp).

questions.stem: After fertilisation, the integuments of the ovule develop into the
questions.explanation: The testa protects the embryo inside the seed.

questions.stem: The micropyle of an ovule is
options: the small opening through which the pollen tube usually enters
the stalk that attaches the ovule to the ovary
the food store of the seed
the part that becomes the root
questions.explanation: In a ripe seed, water enters through the micropyle at the start of germination.

questions.stem: The cashew "apple" is called a false fruit because
options: it contains no seed at all
its fleshy part develops from the swollen flower stalk, not the ovary
it is a seed, not a fruit
questions.explanation: The true fruit is the kidney-shaped nut, which develops from the ovary.

questions.stem: Fruits such as those of Tridax, which carry a parachute of fine hairs, are dispersed by
questions.explanation: The hairs increase air resistance so that the fruit drifts a long way.

questions.stem: The dry pods of many legumes split open suddenly and throw out their seeds. This is
questions.explanation: As the pod dries, tension builds up in its walls until they twist apart.

questions.stem: The coconut is well adapted for dispersal by
options: wind, because it is very light
water, because its fibrous mesocarp traps air and lets it float
questions.explanation: Coconuts can float across seas and grow on distant shores.

questions.stem: The testes of a mammal produce
questions.explanation: Testosterone controls male secondary sexual characteristics.

questions.stem: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the
questions.explanation: The fertilised egg then moves down to the uterus.

questions.stem: In humans, the embryo becomes implanted in the
questions.explanation: The thickened, blood-rich lining of the uterus receives the embryo.

questions.stem: One function of the placenta is to
options: allow food, oxygen and wastes to pass between mother and fetus
mix the blood of mother and fetus directly
protect the fetus from all drugs and viruses
questions.explanation: Substances diffuse across the thin placental membranes. Some harmful drugs and viruses can still cross.

questions.stem: The amniotic fluid around a developing fetus
questions.explanation: The fluid-filled amniotic sac also allows the fetus to move freely.

questions.stem: In a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, ovulation usually occurs on about day
questions.explanation: Day 1 is the first day of menstruation. Ovulation is usually around the middle of the cycle.

questions.stem: Ovulation is triggered by a sudden rise in the level of
questions.explanation: LH is released by the anterior pituitary gland.

questions.stem: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes mainly
questions.explanation: Progesterone keeps the lining of the uterus thick, ready for implantation.

questions.stem: The sperm duct (vas deferens) carries sperm from the
questions.explanation: Along the way, fluids from the seminal vesicles and prostate gland are added to form semen.

questions.stem: The seminal vesicles and prostate gland
options: produce fluids that nourish the sperm and help them to swim
questions.explanation: These fluids make up most of the volume of semen.

questions.stem: In flowering plants, the male gametes are formed inside the
questions.explanation: The male nuclei travel down the pollen tube to reach the ovule.

questions.stem: The umbilical cord
options: connects the uterus to the ovary
holds the fetus in the amniotic fluid but carries no blood
carries blood between the fetus and the placenta
questions.explanation: It contains umbilical arteries and a vein.

questions.stem: The blood of the mother and the blood of the fetus do not mix directly in the placenta. One important reason is that
options: the mother's blood contains no oxygen
the mother's higher blood pressure could damage the fetus, and the two may belong to incompatible blood groups
fetal blood does not contain red cells
questions.explanation: Separate circulations protect the fetus while still allowing exchange of materials by diffusion.

questions.stem: In biology, growth is best defined as
options: a permanent increase in the size or dry mass of an organism
a temporary increase in volume due to water uptake
the loss of mass during respiration
questions.explanation: Taking in water alone (swelling) is reversible and is not true growth.

questions.stem: Which conditions are necessary for seeds to germinate?
options: Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature
questions.explanation: Most seeds germinate in the dark, and soil is not essential (they germinate on wet cotton wool).

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT usually needed for the germination of most seeds?
questions.explanation: Seeds use their stored food until the shoot reaches the light.

questions.stem: In epigeal germination, as in the bean,
options: the cotyledons stay below the ground
the cotyledons are carried above the ground
questions.explanation: The hypocotyl lengthens and pulls the cotyledons up into the light.

questions.stem: In hypogeal germination, as in maize,
options: the cotyledons are pushed above the soil
the cotyledon stays below the soil surface
questions.explanation: Here it is the epicotyl (or coleoptile) that lengthens, so the food store stays underground.

questions.stem: In a germinating seed, the plumule develops into the
questions.explanation: The radicle forms the root and the plumule forms the shoot.

questions.stem: The first structure to emerge from a germinating seed is usually the
questions.explanation: The young root anchors the seedling and starts absorbing water.

questions.stem: During the germination of a maize grain, starch stored in the endosperm is converted to
questions.explanation: Soluble sugars can be carried to the growing embryo, where they are used for respiration and growth.

questions.stem: The dry mass of a seedling decreases for the first few days of germination and then increases. The early decrease is because
options: stored food is used up in respiration before the leaves can photosynthesise
questions.explanation: Respiration releases CO2 and so reduces dry mass. Once photosynthesis exceeds respiration, the dry mass rises.

questions.stem: In flowering plants, increase in length takes place mainly at the
options: apical meristems at the tips of shoots and roots
questions.explanation: Cells at the tips divide by mitosis and then lengthen.

questions.stem: Seed dormancy is a condition in which a seed
options: does not germinate even when conditions are favourable
questions.explanation: Dormancy helps seeds survive unfavourable seasons.

questions.stem: Seeds are placed in water that has been boiled and cooled and is covered with a layer of oil. They fail to germinate because
options: there is no oxygen available for respiration
questions.explanation: Boiling drives out dissolved oxygen, and the oil stops more from dissolving.

questions.stem: The central nervous system is made up of the
questions.explanation: The nerves outside the CNS form the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and muscular movement?
questions.explanation: Damage to the cerebellum causes poor balance and clumsy movements.

questions.stem: The medulla oblongata controls
questions.explanation: It controls vital involuntary activities.

questions.stem: Intelligence, memory, reasoning and voluntary actions are controlled by the
questions.explanation: The cerebrum is the largest part of the human brain.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain monitors and controls body temperature and thirst?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus detects changes in the blood and also controls the pituitary gland.

questions.stem: A sensory neurone carries impulses from
options: the central nervous system to muscles
receptors to the central nervous system
questions.explanation: Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.

questions.stem: The myelin sheath around many nerve fibres
options: insulates the fibre and speeds up the conduction of impulses
questions.explanation: Impulses jump between the gaps in the sheath, which makes conduction much faster.

questions.stem: A nerve impulse passes across a synapse by
options: the release of a chemical transmitter that diffuses across the gap
questions.explanation: The neurotransmitter, such as acetylcholine, binds to receptors on the next neurone.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the correct pathway of a simple reflex arc?
options: Effector -> motor neurone -> relay neurone -> sensory neurone -> receptor
Receptor -> motor neurone -> sensory neurone -> effector
Receptor -> sensory neurone -> relay neurone -> motor neurone -> effector
questions.explanation: The impulse goes from detection, through the spinal cord, to the response.

questions.stem: The knee-jerk response is an example of
questions.explanation: It is fast and automatic and passes through the spinal cord without conscious thought.

questions.stem: Pupils begin to salivate when the lunch bell rings, before they see any food. This is an example of
questions.explanation: The response has been learnt by linking the bell with food.

questions.stem: The autonomic nervous system controls
options: involuntary activities such as heartbeat and the movements of the gut
the voluntary movement of the limbs
questions.explanation: Its sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions have opposite effects.

questions.stem: The rods in the retina are
options: sensitive to dim light but do not detect colour
questions.explanation: Rods allow vision at night, in black and white.

questions.stem: Colour vision in bright light depends on the
questions.explanation: There are cones that respond to red, green and blue light.

questions.stem: The fovea (yellow spot) of the eye is the region where
options: the optic nerve leaves the eye
cones are most concentrated, so vision is sharpest
questions.explanation: Light from whatever we look at directly is focused onto the fovea.

questions.stem: The blind spot of the eye has no vision because
options: it has no rods or cones, since the optic nerve leaves the eye there
it is covered by the iris
it is filled with aqueous humour
questions.explanation: There are no photoreceptors at this point, so images falling on it are not detected.

questions.stem: When the eye focuses on a near object, the ciliary muscles contract and the lens becomes
questions.explanation: The suspensory ligaments slacken, so the elastic lens becomes rounder and bends light more.

questions.stem: In bright light, the pupil of the eye
questions.explanation: The circular muscles of the iris contract, so less light enters and the retina is protected.

questions.stem: Short sight (myopia) can be corrected with
questions.explanation: In myopia, images form in front of the retina, and a diverging lens moves them back onto it.

questions.stem: Long sight (hypermetropia) can be corrected with
questions.explanation: In long sight, images would form behind the retina, and a converging lens brings them forward.

questions.stem: In the mammalian ear, the semicircular canals are concerned with
questions.explanation: Fluid moving in the canals tells the brain about movements of the head. The cochlea is for hearing.

questions.stem: The ear ossicles (hammer, anvil and stirrup)
options: pass vibrations from the eardrum to the oval window and amplify them
equalise pressure on both sides of the eardrum
questions.explanation: They act as levers that increase the force of the vibrations.

questions.stem: The Eustachian tube
options: equalises the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum
questions.explanation: It connects the middle ear to the throat. Swallowing opens it, which is why ears "pop" on an aeroplane.

questions.stem: The taste buds on the tongue are chemoreceptors that detect
options: sweet, sour, salty and bitter tastes
questions.explanation: Taste receptors respond to chemicals dissolved in saliva.

questions.stem: Insulin, produced by the pancreas,
options: lowers the level of glucose in the blood
raises the level of glucose in the blood
questions.explanation: Insulin causes the liver and muscles to take up glucose and store it as glycogen.

questions.stem: Adrenaline, secreted by the adrenal glands in times of fear or danger,
options: increases heart rate and the level of glucose in the blood
questions.explanation: It prepares the body for "fight or flight".

questions.stem: Thyroxine, secreted by the thyroid gland,
options: controls the level of calcium in the blood
controls water reabsorption in the kidneys
questions.explanation: Too little thyroxine in children causes cretinism, and too little in adults causes sluggishness.

questions.stem: The pituitary gland is called the master gland because it
options: is the largest gland in the body
secretes hormones that control several other endocrine glands
produces all the hormones of the body
questions.explanation: For example, it makes TSH (which acts on the thyroid) and FSH and LH (which act on the gonads).

questions.stem: The parathyroid hormone regulates the level of
questions.explanation: It raises the level of calcium in the blood by acting on the bones, kidneys and gut.

questions.stem: Too much growth hormone produced during childhood causes
questions.explanation: Growth hormone from the pituitary stimulates growth of the long bones.

questions.stem: Which plant hormone is mainly responsible for stem elongation and for breaking seed dormancy?
questions.explanation: Gibberellins also stimulate the production of amylase in germinating cereal grains.

questions.stem: Abscisic acid in plants
options: promotes dormancy and the closing of stomata
questions.explanation: It is a growth inhibitor that helps plants cope with stress such as drought.

questions.stem: Cytokinins are plant hormones that mainly
questions.explanation: Cytokinins work together with auxins to control growth and the formation of new organs.

questions.stem: Homeostasis is the
options: response of a plant to light
maintenance of a constant internal environment in the body
questions.explanation: Body temperature, blood glucose and water balance are kept within narrow limits.

questions.stem: When the human body becomes too hot,
options: arterioles in the skin narrow and the person shivers
arterioles in the skin widen (vasodilation) and sweating increases
the hairs on the skin stand up
questions.explanation: More blood flows near the skin surface and loses heat, and sweat evaporating from the skin cools it.

questions.stem: Shivering in a cold environment helps to
options: produce heat through rapid contractions of the muscles
questions.explanation: Respiration in the contracting muscles releases heat.

questions.stem: After a person drinks a large volume of water, the
options: secretion of ADH increases, so a small volume of concentrated urine is produced
secretion of ADH decreases, so a large volume of dilute urine is produced
questions.explanation: With less ADH, the collecting ducts reabsorb less water, so the excess water is removed.

questions.stem: Testosterone, the male sex hormone, is produced in the
questions.explanation: It brings about male secondary sexual characteristics such as a deeper voice and the growth of facial hair.

questions.topic: Factors affecting the distribution of organisms
questions.stem: Which of these is an abiotic factor in an ecosystem?
